theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In a public body, what does "workplace diversity" mainly refer to?
options: The range of services the body offers to members of the public each year
The differences between people in the workforce and the public served
The number of different departments within the ministry
The variety of computer systems used by the staff

questions.stem: What is the difference between diversity and inclusion?
options: Diversity is the mix of people; inclusion is how involved they feel
Diversity applies to the public; inclusion applies only to the staff
Diversity is about age only; inclusion is about disability only
They mean the same thing and the words can be swapped

questions.stem: Which is a less visible dimension of diversity that a manager may not know about unless a person shares it?
options: The parish where the officer works
The officer's job title and grade
A long-term health condition
The officer's working hours

questions.stem: A ministry's policy team is made up entirely of people of the same age and background from Kingston. What is the main risk for its policies?
options: The team will work too slowly to meet its deadlines
The team will spend too much of the budget on travel to the parishes
The team will disagree too often to reach decisions
The team may miss the needs of other groups in the country

questions.stem: Which is the strongest business reason for a public agency to have a workforce that reflects the people it serves?
options: It understands and serves the public better
It makes the agency's reports shorter
It removes the need for staff training
It lets the agency pay lower salaries

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a public body's legal position on diversity in Jamaica?
options: Laws on rights and fair treatment apply only to private firms, never to public bodies
It must respect the rights in the Constitution and laws such as those on disability
There are no laws that touch on fair treatment of staff or the public
Only the agency's own rules apply, and these may be ignored if busy

questions.stem: A manager is unsure whether a planned change to a recruitment rule is lawful. What should she do?
options: Go ahead and wait to see if anyone complains
Ask a colleague in another unit what they think
Seek advice from the human resource or legal unit
Drop the change and keep the old rule for ever

questions.stem: A panel member says, "Older applicants struggle with computers, so we should pick the younger one." What is this an example of?
options: A fair judgement based on test results
A stereotype that leads to unfair bias
A reasonable accommodation for age
A positive action measure for youth

questions.stem: What does the term "unconscious bias" mean in the workplace?
options: Bias that a person shows only when tired
Bias written into an organisation's policy
Bias shown only against people one has never met in person
Attitudes people hold without being aware of them

questions.stem: Which step most reduces unconscious bias when an agency shortlists applicants?
options: Scoring each application against the same written criteria
Letting one senior manager choose whom to shortlist alone
Reading the applicant's photo and home address before anything else
Picking applicants who are most like the current team

questions.stem: A municipal corporation refuses to interview a qualified applicant because she is pregnant. What kind of discrimination is this?
options: Indirect discrimination
Positive action
Direct discrimination
Reasonable accommodation

questions.stem: An agency requires all field officers to be at least 1.8 m tall, though height is not needed for the job. Few women can meet it. What is this most likely to be?
options: Positive action for women
A fair occupational requirement
Direct discrimination by name
Indirect discrimination

questions.stem: An officer living with HIV tells his supervisor about his condition in confidence. What should the supervisor do?
options: Keep it confidential and ask what support, if any, he needs
Tell the team so they can take extra precautions when working with him
Move him to a desk away from the public at once
Report it to the director so his file can be marked

questions.stem: A group of staff keep making jokes about a colleague's rural accent and calling her names. What should the manager do?
options: Leave it, because jokes are part of office life
Tell the colleague to try to change her accent
Stop it, deal with it under policy and support her
Wait until the colleague makes a formal complaint

questions.stem: Why should a public body have a clear policy and procedure on harassment, including sexual harassment?
options: So that staff never have to work closely with each other on any task
So staff know what is not allowed and how to report it safely
So the manager can avoid dealing with any complaints
So that complaints can only be made by senior officers

questions.stem: A ministry wants more applicants from rural parishes for its graduate trainee posts. Which step is most likely to help?
options: Advertise only in one Kingston newspaper
Accept applications only in person in Kingston
Advertise widely, including online and in rural areas
Ask current staff to suggest their own relatives and friends for the posts

questions.stem: Why should an interview panel in a public body include people of different backgrounds where possible?
options: It reduces the effect of any one person's bias
It makes the interviews last a shorter time
It means no scoring sheet will be needed
It lets the panel ask each applicant different questions

questions.stem: Which interview question should NOT be asked of applicants for a clerical post?
options: Tell us about a time you met a tight deadline in a past job.
How would you deal with an angry member of the public?
Which filing systems have you used in past work?
Are you planning to have children in the next few years?

questions.stem: A newly hired officer who is partially sighted needs screen-reading software and a larger monitor. What is this kind of change usually called?
options: A reasonable accommodation
Positive discrimination
A disciplinary measure
A probation condition

questions.stem: An officer who uses a wheelchair is posted to a unit on the second floor of a building with no lift. What is the best first step?
options: Ask the officer to find another job in a new building
Tell the officer to manage the stairs with help from staff
Talk with the officer and arrange a ground-floor workspace
Leave the officer's post empty until a lift is built

questions.stem: A Deaf member of the public visits a tax office to ask about a bill. Which service would best meet her needs?
options: Speak slowly and very loudly to her at the counter in front of others
Ask her to come back with a family member
Give her a leaflet and ask her to go home
Use a Jamaican Sign Language interpreter or written exchange

questions.stem: A public hospital's forms are written in long legal language. Many patients struggle to complete them. What is the best change?
options: Add more pages of notes explaining every term
Rewrite them in plain language and offer help to complete them
Ask patients to bring a lawyer to help them
Translate them into one foreign language only and keep the legal wording

questions.stem: Which is the most useful first step when a parish office plans to make its services more accessible?
options: Ask users with different needs what barriers they meet
Buy new furniture for the waiting area at once
Copy the plan used by a government office in another country
Ask only the front-line staff what they prefer

questions.stem: An officer writes a public notice using words such as "chairman", "manpower" and "he" for every applicant. Which change makes it more inclusive?
options: Add "(or she)" in small print at the end
Use "chair", "staff" and "applicants" or "they"
Remove the notice and send no notice at all
Keep the words, because everyone understands them

questions.stem: A community officer meets residents in a rural district who are more comfortable speaking Jamaican Creole (Patois). What is the most respectful approach?
options: Insist that everyone speak formal English only
Bring a written speech and avoid questions
Ask the residents to send a spokesperson to Kingston
Use plain words and let residents speak as they prefer

questions.stem: A Seventh-day Adventist officer asks not to be rostered from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. What should the manager do?
options: Refuse, because the roster must treat everyone the same
Consider the request fairly and adjust the roster if work allows
Tell the officer to change jobs if the roster is a problem for his faith
Agree, but give the officer the worst shifts in return

questions.stem: An agency's staff party includes only food that some staff cannot eat for religious reasons. What would have been better?
options: Cancel all staff parties from now on
Ask those staff to bring their own food
Ask staff about dietary needs when planning
Hold separate parties for each religion

questions.stem: A unit has several officers near retirement and many new graduates. Which approach best uses this age mix?
options: Keep the two groups apart to avoid any conflict
Pair them so each group learns from the other
Give all the new projects to the graduates only
Encourage the older officers to retire early

questions.stem: In a public body, 36 of the 120 managers are women. What percentage of managers are women?
Of 200 applicants for agency posts, 30 said they had a disability. Of the 20 people hired, 1 had a disability. What does this suggest?
options: The process should be reviewed for possible barriers
The process is clearly fair to applicants with disabilities
Applicants with disabilities are less able to do the work
The agency should stop asking about disability at all

questions.stem: Why should staff diversity data in a public body be collected voluntarily and kept confidential?
options: So that managers can use it to decide promotions
So that it can be shared freely with the public
So staff trust it and the data protection law is met
So that the human resource unit has much less work to do

questions.stem: Which is the best use of staff survey results that show staff with disabilities feel less included?
options: File the results and wait for next year's survey
Name the staff who answered negatively
Ask managers to explain their scores to the press
Discuss them with staff and agree actions to improve

questions.stem: What should a public body's diversity and inclusion policy contain?
options: Aims, responsibilities, how to raise concerns and how it is monitored
A full list of all staff by age, religion and health condition
A promise that every group will be hired in exactly equal numbers each year
The names of staff who have made complaints in the past

questions.stem: A diversity policy was launched two years ago, but staff have never heard of it. What should the manager do first?
options: Write a new and much longer policy straight away
Communicate it, train staff and build it into routines
Wait until the next review date before acting
Ask staff to read it on the intranet in their own time

questions.stem: How can a manager best show that she values diversity in her unit?
options: By talking about diversity once a year at the staff Christmas party
By putting a poster about diversity on the wall
By asking only senior staff for their opinions
By seeking different views and treating all staff fairly

questions.stem: In team meetings, a few confident officers speak most of the time while quieter officers say little. What should the chair do?
options: Invite each person's view in turn and use other ways to share ideas
Let the confident officers lead the talk, as they usually have the best ideas
Ask the quieter officers to speak more often after the meeting
Hold meetings less often so fewer people need to speak

questions.stem: What is "tokenism" in diversity work?
options: Rewarding staff with tokens for good attendance
Making a small, surface effort to look inclusive
Measuring the number of staff in each group
Holding a yearly event to celebrate culture

questions.stem: A public body offers a mentoring scheme open to all, but promotes it especially to women officers, who are under-represented in senior posts. What is this?
options: Unlawful favouritism towards women
Tokenism with no real purpose
Lawful positive action to widen access
Direct discrimination against men

questions.stem: Which approach to diversity training is most likely to change behaviour?
options: A single lecture with a long list of rules
Practical cases, discussion and follow-up in teams
An email asking staff to read the policy
A poster in the canteen with the policy's title

questions.stem: A ministry is designing a new youth employment programme. Which step best brings in diverse views?
options: Consult youth groups, disability groups and rural communities
Ask the minister's own advisers to design the whole programme alone
Copy last year's programme and change the dates
Ask only the young people who already work there

questions.stem: An officer complains that she was passed over for promotion because of her religion. What should the manager do first?
options: Tell her she is being too sensitive about it
Ask the promoted officer to step down at once
Discuss the complaint with her friends in the unit
Take it seriously and follow the grievance procedure

questions.stem: Why must a public body protect staff from bad treatment after they raise a diversity concern in good faith?
options: So that the concern can be dropped more quickly
So that the manager does not need to investigate
So staff are not afraid to report problems
So that the complaint can be kept secret from HR

questions.stem: A single father in an agency asks to start work an hour later so he can take his child to school. What is the best response?
options: Refuse, because it would be unfair to others
Agree only if he takes a cut in pay
Consider it fairly against the needs of the work
Tell him to ask a relative to help instead

questions.stem: Which measure best shows whether a public body's diversity actions are working?
options: The number of diversity posters on its walls and notice boards
The cost of the diversity training last year
The number of pages in its diversity policy
Trends in inclusion survey scores and staff mix over time

questions.stem: An agency's yearly review shows that complaints of unfair treatment have fallen, but so have survey responses. What is the soundest conclusion?
options: The fall in complaints may not mean less unfair treatment
Unfair treatment has clearly ended in the agency
The survey should be stopped because so few staff now answer it
Diversity work is no longer needed in the agency

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term describes attitudes or beliefs people hold about others without being aware of them?
What one word means a fixed, over-simple belief about what all members of a group are like?
What one word describes making sure every person feels valued, respected and able to take part fully?
What type of discrimination is it when a rule applies to everyone but puts one group at an unfair disadvantage?
What type of discrimination is it when a person is treated less well openly because of a personal characteristic?
What two-word term describes a change to work or the workplace that allows a person with a disability to do the job?
What is the name of the sign language used by Deaf people in Jamaica?
What one word describes how easily people of all abilities can reach and use a building, service or document?
What word describes unwanted conduct that violates a person's dignity or creates a hostile setting for them?
What word describes a small, surface effort made only to look inclusive, such as one token appointment?
What two-word term describes lawful steps that encourage under-represented groups to apply or develop, without lowering standards?
In a ministry, 48 of the 160 senior officers are men. What percentage of senior officers are men?
Of 250 applicants, 50 lived in rural parishes. What percentage of applicants were rural?
What two-word term describes a planned review of an organisation's workforce, policies and services to find gaps in diversity and inclusion?
What one word means an unfair opinion formed about a person or group before knowing the facts?

essays.stem: Explain the benefits of a diverse and inclusive workforce for a Jamaican public body, and the problems that can arise if diversity is not well managed.
essays.modelAnswer: A diverse workforce includes people of different ages, genders, abilities, faiths, social backgrounds and parishes. For a public body this brings clear benefits. Staff who reflect the public understand its needs better, so services and policies fit real lives, for example in rural areas or for persons with disabilities. Different views lead to better problem-solving and fewer blind spots in decisions. Members of the public trust a body more when they see people like themselves in it. An inclusive workplace also attracts and keeps talented staff, and people who feel valued work harder and stay longer. However, diversity must be managed well. Without inclusion, staff may form cliques, misunderstandings and conflict can grow, and some groups may feel left out or face harassment. Unconscious bias can creep into recruitment, rosters or promotion, leading to unfair treatment, grievances and possible breaches of the law. The body may also lose the benefits of different views if only some voices are heard. Good leadership, clear policy, training and fair procedures are needed to gain the benefits and avoid the problems.
markingPoints: Explains that a workforce reflecting the public understands and serves it better
Explains benefits of different views for decisions and problem-solving
Explains benefits for public trust and for attracting and keeping staff
Explains problems when poorly managed: conflict, exclusion, harassment or bias
Notes the need for leadership, policy, training and fair procedures

essays.stem: A statutory body wants its recruitment process to be fair to applicants of all backgrounds. Recommend changes it should make at each stage, from advertising to appointment.
essays.modelAnswer: At the planning stage, the body should check that the job description and person specification list only what the job really needs, removing needless conditions such as height or a degree for a post that does not need one. At the advertising stage, it should advertise widely, online, in newspapers, through community groups and in rural parishes, use plain and inclusive language, state that it welcomes applicants from all backgrounds, and offer accessible formats and help on request. At shortlisting, it should score every application against the same written criteria, using a panel rather than one person, and could remove names and addresses from forms to reduce bias. At interview, it should use a diverse, trained panel, ask every applicant the same job-related questions, score answers against agreed standards and make reasonable accommodations, such as a ground-floor room or extra time. Questions about family plans, religion or health that are not job-related should not be asked. At appointment, the decision should be based on the scores and recorded. Finally, the body should monitor applicant and appointment data to find any group that is falling out of the process.
markingPoints: Checks job requirements and removes needless conditions
Advertises widely in inclusive, accessible ways
Shortlists against written criteria with a panel, possibly anonymised
Uses a diverse trained panel, the same job-related questions and accommodations
Records decisions and monitors applicant data for barriers

essays.stem: Plan how a municipal corporation's customer service centre could make its services accessible to persons with disabilities.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by consulting persons with disabilities and disability organisations about the barriers they face, and by walking through the service myself with a checklist. For physical access, I would check for a ramp and handrails at the entrance, a clear route to the counter, a lower counter section, accessible toilets, seating for those who cannot stand long, and reserved parking near the door. For communication, I would offer forms in large print and plain language, arrange a Jamaican Sign Language interpreter on request or set times, keep pen and paper ready for written exchange, and make sure the website works with screen-reading software. I would let people book appointments by phone, text or online so they do not have to queue. Staff would be trained in disability awareness, how to offer help respectfully, and how to communicate with Deaf, blind or partially sighted customers. I would make sure emergency procedures include persons with disabilities. Finally, I would set measures such as customer feedback from persons with disabilities, review progress each year and budget for further improvements.
markingPoints: Consults persons with disabilities and audits the service first
Plans physical access improvements (ramp, counter, toilets, seating, parking)
Plans communication access (large print, plain language, sign language, accessible website)
Includes staff training and emergency procedures that include persons with disabilities
Sets measures, gathers feedback and reviews progress

essays.stem: Explain how stereotypes and unconscious bias can affect decisions in a public agency, and describe steps a manager can take to reduce their effect.
essays.modelAnswer: Stereotypes are over-simple beliefs about groups, such as "older staff cannot learn new technology" or "people from certain communities are unreliable". Unconscious bias is when we hold such views without knowing it, often preferring people who are like us. In a public agency these can affect many decisions. In recruitment, a panel may favour an applicant from a familiar school or area. In allocating work, a manager may give the best projects to people she feels comfortable with. In serving the public, an officer may treat a customer from an inner-city community with suspicion. The result is unfair treatment, lost talent and poorer service, and it may breach the law. A manager can reduce the effect by using clear, written criteria and scoring for decisions, and by using panels rather than one person. She can slow down important decisions and ask, "Would I decide the same way if this person were from another group?" She can arrange training that helps staff recognise bias, collect data to spot patterns, invite challenge from colleagues, and lead by example in how she speaks about others.
markingPoints: Explains stereotypes and unconscious bias clearly
Gives examples of their effect in recruitment, work allocation or service
Explains the results: unfairness, lost talent, poorer service, legal risk
Recommends written criteria, scoring and panels
Recommends reflection, training, data monitoring, challenge and leading by example

essays.stem: Describe how you would develop and launch a diversity and inclusion policy for a government agency of 300 staff.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by gathering facts: staff data, a short staff survey on inclusion, complaint records, and the views of staff groups and service users. I would check the relevant laws, such as the rights in the Constitution and the disability law, with the legal unit, and look at the government's own policies so ours fits them. I would then form a small working group with staff from different levels, units and backgrounds to draft the policy. It would state the agency's commitment and aims, what fair treatment means in recruitment, training, promotion and services, the duties of managers and staff, how to raise a concern safely, and how progress will be measured and reported. The draft would be shared for comment with staff and, where suitable, community groups, and then approved by senior management. For the launch, the head of the agency would introduce it in person to show it matters. Managers would brief their teams, and all staff would receive short, practical training. The policy would be built into induction, recruitment and appraisal, and reviewed each year using the measures it set.
markingPoints: Gathers data and staff and user views first
Checks the law and government policy with expert advice
Uses a diverse working group and sets out the policy's content
Consults on the draft and obtains senior approval
Launches it with visible leadership, briefings and training, builds it into routines and reviews it

essays.stem: An officer tells you, her manager, that colleagues often make remarks about her disability and leave her out of team lunches. Describe how you would respond.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank her for telling me, listen carefully and take her concern seriously. I would ask what has happened, when, who was involved and how it has affected her, and I would ask what she would like to happen. I would explain the options under the agency's policy: informal action, where I speak to those involved, or a formal complaint, which leads to an investigation. I would keep the matter confidential, sharing it only with those who need to know, and make clear that she will not be treated badly for raising it. I would make a written note of what she said and agree when we will speak again. If she chose the informal route, I would speak privately with the colleagues, describe the behaviour and its effect, make clear it is not acceptable under our policy, and ask them to stop. If the behaviour is serious or continues, I would seek human resource advice and follow the formal procedure. I would also check on her wellbeing, point her to support, and consider team training on disability awareness and respectful conduct.
markingPoints: Listens, takes the concern seriously and asks what she wants
Explains informal and formal options under policy
Keeps the matter confidential and protects her from bad treatment
Acts on the behaviour, using HR advice and the formal procedure if needed
Records the facts, follows up and supports her and the wider team

essays.stem: Evaluate the role of a senior manager in promoting diversity across a ministry, and recommend the actions that would make the greatest difference.
essays.modelAnswer: Senior managers set the tone for the whole ministry. Staff watch what leaders do more than what policies say, so a senior manager who speaks respectfully, seeks different views and deals firmly with unfair treatment shows that diversity matters. Senior managers also control resources, approve policies and decide promotions and key appointments, so they can remove barriers or keep them in place. If they treat diversity as a box to tick, staff will too, and policies will have little effect. The actions that would make the greatest difference are, first, to make inclusion part of the ministry's plan, with clear goals and measures reported to the executive. Second, to make sure recruitment and promotion panels use fair criteria and to check the results by group. Third, to hold managers accountable for inclusion in their appraisals. Fourth, to support mentoring and development for under-represented groups. Fifth, to listen directly to staff, for example through open forums and staff surveys, and act on what is heard. Finally, the manager should model inclusive behaviour every day, in meetings, decisions and language.
markingPoints: Explains that senior managers set the tone and are role models
Explains that they control policy, resources and key decisions
Recommends building inclusion into plans with goals and measures
Recommends fair recruitment and promotion, manager accountability or mentoring
Recommends listening to staff, acting on it and modelling inclusive behaviour daily

essays.stem: Compare two ways of raising diversity awareness among staff of a public body: a one-off lecture and an ongoing programme. Recommend which to use and why.
essays.modelAnswer: A one-off lecture brings all staff together for an hour or two to hear about the policy, the law and the meaning of diversity and inclusion. It is quick, cheap and reaches many people at once, and it can be useful to launch a policy. But people forget most of what they hear in a lecture, it gives little chance to practise or discuss real situations, and it may feel like a box-ticking exercise. Some staff may even become defensive if they feel blamed. An ongoing programme spreads learning over time. It might include a short introduction, then team sessions using real cases from the workplace, role plays on handling remarks or serving customers with different needs, manager coaching, and follow-up discussions in team meetings. It costs more time and needs planning, but it allows staff to reflect, practise and change habits, and it shows the body is serious. I would recommend an ongoing programme, perhaps launched with a short talk by the head of the body, because the aim is to change behaviour, not just to share information, and behaviour changes through practice and reinforcement.
markingPoints: Describes the one-off lecture with its strengths
Explains its weaknesses: forgetting, no practice, box-ticking
Describes an ongoing programme and its methods
Weighs the extra cost of the programme against its benefits
Recommends an ongoing programme, justified by the aim of changing behaviour

essays.stem: A ministry is planning a new community health programme for all parishes. Explain how it should involve diverse groups in the design, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The ministry should first map who the programme will affect: urban and rural residents, older people, young people, persons with disabilities, people with low literacy, different faith groups and people living with long-term illness. It should then plan ways to reach each group. These might include public meetings in different parishes at times and places people can reach, focus groups with youth and seniors, meetings with disability and faith organisations, a short survey in plain language, and talks with community health aides and church and community leaders who know local needs. Meetings should be accessible, with sign language interpreters and large-print materials when needed, and staff should welcome views in Jamaican Creole as well as English. The ministry should record what it hears, show how the views changed the design, and report back to the communities. This matters because people know their own needs best. A programme designed only by head office may miss real barriers, such as transport costs in rural areas or clinic hours that clash with work. Involving people builds trust and ownership, so the programme is more likely to be used and to succeed.
markingPoints: Identifies the range of groups the programme will affect
Describes suitable ways to reach each group, including community leaders
Makes consultation accessible (venues, times, interpreters, plain language, Creole)
Records views, shows how they changed the design and reports back
Explains why it matters: real needs, avoiding barriers, trust and use

essays.stem: Describe how a public body should measure and report its progress in promoting diversity, and explain the care needed when collecting the data.
essays.modelAnswer: The body should first set clear goals, such as more women in senior posts, better access for persons with disabilities or higher inclusion scores, and choose measures for each. Useful measures include the mix of staff at each grade compared with the public served, applicant and appointment data by group, promotion and training rates, results of an annual inclusion survey, the number and outcome of complaints, and feedback from members of the public with different needs. It should compare results with a baseline and look at trends over several years, not one year alone. Results should be reported to senior management and, in summary, to staff, with actions agreed for any gaps. Great care is needed with the data. Personal details such as disability, religion or health are sensitive, so staff should give them voluntarily, know why they are collected and how they will be used, and be able to decline. The data must be stored securely, with limited access, and reported only in groups large enough that no person can be identified, in line with the data protection law.
markingPoints: Sets clear goals and matching measures
Uses a range of measures: staff mix, recruitment, promotion, surveys, complaints, public feedback
Compares with a baseline and trends, and reports with actions
Collects sensitive data voluntarily with a clear purpose
Stores data securely and reports it so no one can be identified, under data protection law

practical1.title: Carry out an inclusion and accessibility audit and write an action plan
practical1.brief: Your group will audit how inclusive and accessible a public service point is. The assessor will give you either permission to audit the Centre's own reception and one classroom, or a case pack with photos and notes of a made-up parish office. As a group, plan the audit, carry it out, and write an action plan for the manager. Give each member a named role: audit lead (writes the audit plan and checklist covering physical access, signs and forms, communication, staff practice and policies), physical access checker (checks entrances, routes, counters, seating and toilets, and measures where safe), communication checker (reviews signs, forms and notices for plain language, print size and inclusive wording, and suggests rewording for one form), policy reviewer (reviews the case policy or a sample notice and notes gaps), and action planner (turns the findings into an action plan with priority, owner, cost level and date). In a group of four, the audit lead also writes the action plan. Every member records findings on the shared checklist. Do not photograph members of the public or staff, only the places and documents.
materials: Audit checklist template (or blank paper to design one)
Computer with word processor software and printer
photos: The audit plan and the completed checklist
An access point being checked, such as the entrance, counter or route (no people)
A form or notice before and after the group's rewording
The group's findings sorted on a flipchart
The finished action plan with priority, owner, cost level and date
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the audit
Audit checklist covers physical access, communication, staff practice and policy
Findings are factual, specific and supported by notes or measurements
Rewording of the form or notice uses plain, inclusive language
Action plan gives realistic priorities, owners, cost levels and dates
Spoke respectfully about all groups throughout the task
safety: Photograph places and documents only, never members of the public or staff
Do not block doors, ramps or routes while checking them; work in pairs near stairs
Keep the audit findings confidential to the group, the assessor and the Centre
Use respectful language about all groups at all times
Share the workload fairly and take a short break

practical2.title: Design and deliver a short diversity awareness session for public officers
practical2.brief: Your group will design and deliver a 20-minute awareness session on promoting diversity for the staff of a made-up public body (for example the customer service unit of a government agency in Spanish Town). The assessor plays the unit head, and other trainees or the assessor act as participants. Give each member a named role: session lead (writes the session plan with aims, timings and activities, and opens and closes the session), content writer (prepares 5 to 8 slides or flipchart pages on what diversity and inclusion mean, unconscious bias and fair treatment), case writer (writes two short workplace scenarios for discussion, such as serving a Deaf customer or a remark about a colleague's religion), materials designer (makes an A3 poster of five inclusive practices for the unit), and evaluator (designs a short feedback form, collects the forms and writes a one-paragraph summary of the results). In a group of four, the session lead also designs the feedback form. Every member presents part of the session.
materials: Computer with presentation software and a projector or screen, or flipchart paper and markers
A3 paper and coloured markers for the poster
Printer and paper for scenarios and feedback forms
photos: The written session plan with aims, timings and activities
The poster of five inclusive practices
The session in progress, showing the set-up (faces only if all agree)
The completed feedback forms and the evaluator's summary
checklist: Took a named role and presented part of the session
Content is accurate, respectful and in plain language
